title: A job pool
description:
Run game jobs on a few worker threads and wait for the results.

```
4 workers, 20 jobs (each sums a range)
results in order: 20 values, total the same as on one thread
time: about 1/4 of running them one by one
```
hints: `std::async` (from `<future>`) runs a function on another thread and hands back a `std::future` for its result: `std::future<long long> f{ std::async(std::launch::async, sumRange, 0, 1000) };` starts the work, and `f.get()` waits for it to finish and returns the value. Keep the futures in a `std::vector` in submission order.
Each `get()` waits for that job only; the others keep running.
requirements: Use `std::async(std::launch::async, ...)` or your own threads with a queue.
Collect `std::future`s and get them in submission order.
Compare the time with running the jobs on one thread.
stretch: Write a real pool: a fixed set of threads, a job queue with a condition variable, and a stop flag.
